articles.title: An 18-year-old used 3D printers to build a shoe-accessories brand before launching a viral beer koozie that made $315,000 in one month
articles.summary: Most teenagers spend high school juggling homework and weekend plans, but Michael Satterlee spent his building a business powered by 3D printers.
articles.body: Most teenagers spend high school juggling homework and weekend plans, but Michael Satterlee spent his building a business powered by 3D printers. What began as a shoe accessories brand became the launchpad for something much bigger, a viral beer koozie that generated more than $300,000 in a single month. His story shows how social media, inexpensive technology, and constant experimentation can help a young founder test ideas without risking much money. It also reveals the lessons that come with fast growth, from hiring help to keeping up with demand. Here is how spare 3D printers became a real business.How an 18-year-old used spare 3D printers from his shoe accessories brand Solefully to start a new businessMichael Satterlee, 18, of Clifton Park, New York, was a full-time high school student when he ran Solefully, a six-figure business that designs and 3D prints unique accessories for Crocs, according to Entrepreneur, which told his story in an as-told-to format. Satterlee told Entrepreneur that he had a bunch of 3D printers from his time working on Solefully and was not using all of them because demand at the time was limited. He asked himself why he did not simply create a different e-commerce store to put those machines to work. After brainstorming, beer koozies, the insulating sleeves that keep a can cold, caught his eye. He wondered how he could make the product better and, more importantly, how he could make it go viral.How Satterlee designed the Beerzooka, a patent-pending beer koozie, and prototyped it in a single dayHis first question was how to make a koozie easier to use. His answer was a design that opens on both the top and the bottom, so cans slide in easily. He then tested ideas for making the product go viral and found that raising the cap slightly makes the can eject when a new one is loaded, much like a shell reloading mechanism. Because he has a lot of experience with computer-aided design, he told Entrepreneur he had a working product within a day, after a couple of printed variations. The product became the Beerzooka; it is a patent-pending creation from his company, Cruise Cup. Satterlee said he has patents and trademarks filed to protect it.How social media, Facebook ads, and viral videos drove Cruise Cup from $100,000 to $315,000 in monthly salesHe carried lessons from his first business into Cruise Cup, including how to structure a product on social media and build a Shopify store. When he posted the Beerzooka online, it drew 50 million views. Cruise Cup launched in August 2025 with about $100,000 in sales that first month, he said. Sales dipped to about $55,000 in September when he began Facebook ads, but organic views weakened. Ramping up paid ads in October brought sales back to $100,000, and November reached $315,000. He told Entrepreneur he tests content on TikTok and Instagram first, and if it works there, it will work on Facebook ads 90 per cent of the time. In December, he cut ad spend entirely to fulfil holiday orders.Why Satterlee wants to manufacture the Beerzooka in metal and urges young entrepreneurs to test every ideaA build plate of three Beerzookas takes 15 hours to print, so he needs many printers, and even with 150 machines, a maximum of 400 cups per day can leave a backlog when a video goes viral. He is now working to manufacture the Beerzooka in stainless steel, which he said would hold drinks cold for more than 12 hours. He runs Cruise Cup, which is entirely self-funded, from a 1,500-square-foot warehouse with two full-time employees, because he said you can only get so far working alone. His advice to young founders is to test as many ideas as possible, since social media and 3D printing are a free playground for testing ads and products.You use AI every day. articles.title: Woman spends up to $380,000 to move her great-great-grandparents’ 112-year-old house to her husband’s family farm
articles.summary: JaSondra Schmidt and her husband, Jason, are restoring a 112-year-old house that belonged to her great-great-grandfather.
articles.body: JaSondra Schmidt and her husband, Jason, are restoring a 112-year-old house that belonged to her great-great-grandfather. It was built in 1914; the home is being relocated six miles to farmland the couple purchased near their existing property in North Dakota.According to an interview with PEOPLE, JaSondra Schmidt shares that their decision brings together two family histories, preserving a home passed down through five generations of JaSondra’s family while allowing the couple and their two daughters to live on land connected to Jason’s grandparents.The project began after years of searching for an old house to renovate. A comment on Facebook eventually led JaSondra to the home she had known about since childhood, giving her an opportunity to preserve her own family’s history.How a Facebook comment led JaSondra Schmidt to her great-great-grandparents’ houseThe couple had spent years looking for an old house to restore. JaSondra grew up in Medina, North Dakota, where passing things on to the next generation was familiar through the agricultural industry. She and Jason had looked at five to seven houses and received offers of free homes on farmland, but none felt right.Their search faced several setbacks. A house they planned to move was no longer an option after flooding in Iowa diverted the movers they had arranged. In 2024, their daughter became ill, forcing the couple to travel frequently between North Dakota and the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota. After nearly a year of travelling back and forth, the couple put their search for a house on hold before picking it up again in late 2025.The 1914 home carries five generations of JaSondra’s family historyIn late 2025, JaSondra came across a Facebook comment in which relatives were discussing a two-storey house. She soon realised it was the home her great-great-grandfather, Freiderich, had owned since it was built in 1914. JaSondra had known about the house since childhood and had seen photographs of it, but she had never visited it.She contacted a relative to ask whether the family planned to sell the property. Another family member had already expressed interest, so JaSondra agreed to wait. Eventually, her relatives agreed to sell the house to JaSondra and Jason, recognising their wish to preserve its history. The purchase gave the couple a chance to restore a home that had been part of JaSondra’s family legacy for generations.How Jason’s family farm became part of the couple’s plan to preserve their family historiesIn August 2025, Jason’s mother was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. She died in February 2026, and about six weeks later, his father was diagnosed with terminal cancer. He then approached the couple about buying his farmstead. JaSondra and Jason initially declined because they had already purchased land and started working on it.Jason’s father had also stated in his will that the couple would have the first option to buy his farm if they changed their minds. Since the property bordered their existing farmland, they decided to reconsider the offer. After spending a weekend walking the land and deciding where to place the house, they agreed to sell their original farmstead and move to the new property.Work on the basement began just four days later. Jason’s grandparents had purchased the land in the early 1940s, making Jason, JaSondra and their two daughters the third generation of his family to live on the property.How a 112-year-old family home was lifted and moved six miles to new farmlandThe house measures approximately 30 feet wide and 60 feet long. Before it could be moved, workers separated it from its original foundation, inserted large steel beams underneath, and used jacks to lift the structure. Rollers fitted to the beams allowed the house to be pushed into position.Its six-mile journey required two power companies to manoeuvre lines along the route. Around 20 relatives gathered to watch the house being moved, just two days after JaSondra’s aunt died from cancer. Once the house reached its new site, it remained elevated on beams and tyres for almost two months while contractors worked on the basement.JaSondra estimates the move itself cost about $40,000, while the concrete for the basement and foundation cost more than $110,000. The overall project is expected to cost between $340,000 and $380,000. The couple have yet to move in and are removing modern additions to restore original-style details and woodwork.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Won’t cremate him till killer is caught': Father of Punjab anti-drug activist who was shot dead during Facebook Live
articles.summary: CHANDIGARH: Bhim Singh, father of anti-drug activist Parminder Singh Jhota and an ex-Armyman, has refused to cremate his son until the killer is caught,
articles.body: CHANDIGARH: Bhim Singh, father of anti-drug activist Parminder Singh Jhota and an ex-Armyman, has refused to cremate his son until the killer is caught, vowing to continue the fight his braveheart son started.Jhota was shot dead by chemist Ashwani Kumar, whom he suspected of selling ‘chitta’ (synthetic drugs), in Mansa on Monday morning. The confrontation was broadcast live on Facebook, and four other people suffered bullet or splinter injuries.Footage showed Kumar following Jhota as he staggered out into the street and took refuge in a shop before opening fire repeatedly. Jhota was hit by three bullets. In the video, he is heard saying, “Mar mainu” (kill me), before Kumar fired. After emptying his magazine, Kumar returned to his shop and fled. Police detained his cousin for allegedly helping him escape.The killing sparked widespread protests in Mansa. Businesses shut down and protesters blocked the Barnala-Sirsa Road. A crowd gathered at Mansa Civil Hospital and clashed with police while demanding that Jhota’s body be taken to the protest site.Bathinda DIG Harjit Singh said the murder stemmed from personal enmity and promised that the accused would be arrested within 24 hours.The killing triggered a political backlash against the AAP government. State finance minister Harpal Singh Cheema and AAP Punjab president Aman Arora condemned the murder, saying it stemmed from personal enmity. Opposition parties accused the government of failing to maintain law and order.Punjab BJP chief Kewal Singh Dhillon wrote to the governor seeking a CBI probe. Congress Leader of Opposition Partap Singh Bajwa said the murder raised serious questions about the AAP government’s ‘Yudh Nasheyan Virudh’ anti-drug campaign. He also referred to the recent suicide of Gulzar Singh and the suicide attempt by Jagseer Singh, alias Jagga, saying the cases should be viewed in the context of concerns over drug availability in Punjab.Akal Takht Jathedar Giani Kuldeep Gargajj described the killing of an activist who had raised his voice against drugs as “a serious matter” and urged the authorities to take note.Police said Jhota and Kumar had a bitter history. In 2023, Jhota had allegedly paraded the chemist through the bazaar with a garland of shoes around his neck, accusing him of selling drugs. Cases were registered against both men.Jhota was arrested on charges of assault, trespass and rioting and remanded in jail. Social and farmers’ organisations staged protests demanding his release. The complainant later approached the court to withdraw the complaint, and Jhota was released on September 11, 2023. The case against Kumar over the alleged sale of prohibited substances remains pending.Jhota continued his anti-drug campaign and had recently raised concerns about medical stores allegedly selling intoxicating pills and synthetic drugs.At around 9.40am on Monday, Jhota went live on social media while confronting Kumar at his pharmacy. He had reportedly met an elderly man who had bought synthetic drugs from a medical store and taken him back to the shop to question Kumar about the alleged sale of prohibited substances. A heated exchange followed before Kumar pulled out a pistol.Mansa Civil Hospital senior medical officer Dr Gurmail Singh said Jhota had been shot twice in the abdomen and once in the right thigh. He died of his injuries. articles.title: Two Arizona brothers, aged 10 and 12, vanished into the desert; trackers followed more than 6 miles of footprints before a helicopter-assisted search found them safe after eight hours
articles.summary: Everyone's childhood often contains memories where they entered into some dangerous territories only to be saved by their parents.
articles.body: Everyone's childhood often contains memories where they entered into some dangerous territories only to be saved by their parents. Often, when one is with their siblings or friends, they end up disregarding the path and are more focused on the company, which can sometimes lead them astray. This is what happened with two young brothers who vanished into the Arizona desert, only to be rescued after a helicopter-assisted search.12-year-old Atom Ward and 10-year-old Jack Ward had vanished when they were playing outside. The officials received a call from a father on October 11, Sunday, reporting he couldn't find his two children who were playing outside, the Mohave County Sheriff's Office said in an alert. At the same time, officials began the search for the two brothers who were last seen by their dad leaving their home on foot in the 1000 block of Birdle Lane in Mohave Valley earlier that afternoon, just before 4 pm.He began tracking his children, including Jack, who happened to be barefoot, said the officials. The family also began searching the surrounding areas and contacting local businesses to determine if the boys had stopped by.After rescue teams arrived, they began a "route and location search", the sheriff's office said. "Trackers confirmed the tracks being followed by the father were the kids' tracks and tracking teams continued following them," the department added.A rescue helicopter from the Arizona Department of Public Safety was dispatched from Phoenix while the Mohave County Sheriff's Office Search and Rescue took over the trail, along with a K-9 Mano with the search and rescue team were aso deployed in the extensive search efforts. By midnight, the little duo was found walking near Spirit Mountain Casino in Mohave Valley, over six miles from their home.“Family met them at that location and brought them back home,” officials said. “They were in good health and the 10-year-old child was still barefoot.”However, it still remains unclear why the children ventured away from home in the first place. For the family and rescuers, the end of the search was a moment to celebrate. “Great job by everyone!” the sheriff’s office said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Texas rejected a settlement that would have cut a proposed data center from 2,523 acres to 1,375; commissioners also denied the developer’s permit appeal as a court fight now looms
articles.summary: Texas' Hood County commissioners have rejected a settlement that would have reduced a proposed data center project from about 2,523 acres to 1,375 acres.
articles.body: Texas' Hood County commissioners have rejected a settlement that would have reduced a proposed data center project from about 2,523 acres to 1,375 acres. They also unanimously denied the developer's appeal against an earlier decision to reject permits for the project, bringing a possible court fight closer. The decisions came on Tuesday, October 13, after hours of public testimony and debate over the Comanche Circle data center project. Developer Sailfish Investors had reportedly offered to reduce the project's size and make commitments on water-efficient cooling, building setbacks, light pollution and road repairs in an effort to reach an agreement with the county.However, commissioners voted 3-1 against the settlement, with Kevin Andrews the only member voting against its rejection. Commissioner Nanette Samuelson was absent. The commissioners later voted unanimously to deny the developer's permit appeal.Why commissioners rejected the settlementThe proposed Comanche Circle campus, led by Sailfish managing partner Ryan Hughes, is planned near the Hood and Somervell county line, close to Dinosaur Valley State Park. Residents raised concerns about the project's possible effects on water supplies, wildlife, nearby properties and local roads. Questions were also raised about drainage, power generation and the project's water source. Opponents argued that the developer had not provided enough information and proper plans.Kevin Andrews said the county should continue discussions with the developer rather than reject the settlement.“We have been offered concessions that we can’t regulate, and I think it would be a good idea for us to continue to negotiate to try to get to terms that work for the county,” Andrews said.The proposed settlement included closed-loop cooling, which is designed to reuse cooling water, along with light pollution controls and other commitments. Hughes also said he would not seek tax incentives if the agreement was approved. However, commissioners rejected the deal and then voted against the appeal of the earlier permit decision.Developer says court action is likelyIn an October 1 email to county officials, Ryan Hughes warned that rejecting the settlement could lead to a lawsuit and potentially leave the project subject to fewer restrictions. Before the vote, he told commissioners, “It looks like we’re unfortunately going to court.”After the decisions, Hughes said he was disappointed but not surprised. In a statement sent to the Fort Worth Star-Telegram, he said he had agreed to reduce the project's size and include water-efficient cooling and light pollution controls.“When Governor Abbott set his commonsense data center standards, I agreed with them wholeheartedly and committed Comanche Circle to them,” Hughes wrote.He added: “I hoped today’s settlement would end this dispute for good. Instead, neighbors lose those protections and taxpayers pay for a court fight the County could have avoided,” he said.Hughes also apologised during the meeting for using profanity in text messages discussed by speakers at the hearing.“That’s how I talk to my friends. That’s how I talk to colleagues. And you know, it’s something that my wife says I really hope to work on. So I definitely apologize for the language and apologize for any insinuations,” he said.Why are residents opposing the projectResidents and local groups, including Protect the Paluxy Valley, have opposed the proposed campus over concerns about its impact on water resources and the surrounding environment. Commissioner Dave Eagle said Hood County has a special designation under state law, known as Subchapter 231K, which covers the watershed that drains into Lake Granbury and the Brazos River.Eagle said the law gives the county powers intended to protect public health and safety and prevent pollution of rivers and lakes. Texas counties are still working out how to regulate large data centre projects while balancing the interests of developers, property owners and local communities.With the settlement rejected and the permit appeal denied, Sailfish Investors faces another setback in its effort to move forward with Comanche Circle. The company had argued that the settlement would allow the project to proceed with additional restrictions, but commissioners chose not to approve the agreement.You use AI every day.
